\paragraph{Model Collapse.}
\citet{shumailov2024collapse} showed that recursive training on model-generated data progressively erodes the tails of learned distributions, a phenomenon they termed \emph{model collapse}.
\citet{dohmatob2024tails} formalized this decay through scaling laws that predict tail erosion as a function of recursive depth, and \citet{dohmatob2024demystified} provided a regression-theoretic analysis of the underlying mechanism.
The self-consuming loop accelerates collapse even under data accumulation~\citep{alemohammad2024mad}, and \citet{dohmatob2025strong} demonstrated that as little as 1\% synthetic contamination suffices to trigger degradation, though \citet{gerstgrasser2024inevitable} showed that preserving all prior real data can delay it.
These studies diagnose collapse through output distributions, benchmark scores, or theoretical scaling laws.
We complement them by tracking collapse through the spectral geometry of internal representations, which requires no text generation or external evaluation.

\paragraph{Spectral Analysis of Representations.}
Random matrix theory (RMT) applied to neural network weights reveals implicit regularization structure in the eigenspectrum~\citep{martin2021implicit}.
Effective rank~\citep{roy2007effectiverank} and its normalized variant RankMe~\citep{rankme2023} have become standard tools for quantifying representational dimensionality.
Recent work has connected spectral properties to training pathologies: \citet{he2025spectral} linked spectral collapse in hidden representations to plasticity loss in continual learning, and \citet{naderi2025mindgap} identified spectral rank collapse in attention matrices as a failure mode of deep transformers.
Most directly relevant, \citet{gu2026sigma} proposed SIGMA, a spectral monitoring framework that tracks singular-value distributions during recursive training on OPT-125M over three generations.
Our work extends SIGMA along several axes.
In \emph{scale}, we track Pythia-410M and pilot Pythia-1B, an order of magnitude larger than OPT-125M.
In \emph{temporal depth}, we follow spectral evolution across 10 recursive generations, revealing a three-phase trajectory (lag--acceleration--saturation) that is not visible at the 3-generation horizon of prior work.
In \emph{methodology}, we move from open-loop observation to closed-loop control: our SLV-based controller actively adjusts the real-data mixing ratio during training (\S\ref{subsec:controller}).
In \emph{metric choice}, we adopt the Spectral Log-Volume (SLV, the log-determinant of the embedding Gram matrix) rather than effective rank or spectral norm, capturing joint changes across the full singular-value spectrum.
Finally, the \emph{signal attenuation paradox}---that successful mixing suppresses the very spectral indicators that would have warned of collapse---is a phenomenon that short-horizon, open-loop monitoring does not encounter.

\paragraph{Early Warning Signals and Critical Transitions.}
The theory of early warning signals (EWS) for critical transitions originates in ecology, where \citet{scheffer2009ews} established that rising autocorrelation and variance precede regime shifts in complex systems.
\citet{scheffer2012anticipating} broadened this framework by identifying architectural features---such as network modularity and feedback structure---that predispose complex systems to tipping points, and argued that combining model-based and observation-based indicators improves anticipation of critical transitions.
\citet{dakos2012methods} developed a methodological toolbox for detecting these signals, and \citet{bury2021deeplearning} showed that deep learning can identify EWS in systems where classical indicators fail.
A central tension in EWS theory is that stabilization interventions suppress the very precursors they rely on~\citep{scheffer2009ews, scheffer2012anticipating}.
We encounter a parallel tension in model collapse, but the failure mode is distinct: ecological stabilization reduces the signal-to-noise ratio while preserving signal direction, whereas real-data mixing reverses the spectral trajectory and eliminates the signal entirely (\S\ref{subsec:controller}).
To our knowledge, this \emph{signal attenuation paradox}---where the intervention that prevents collapse simultaneously destroys the spectral indicator that would have predicted it---has no direct analogue in the ecological EWS literature and constitutes a novel contribution to the broader theory of early warning signals.
\citet{he2025spectral} provides a bridge between these domains by connecting spectral collapse to critical transitions in continual learning.

\paragraph{Data Mixing for LLM Training.}
A growing body of work studies how training data composition shapes language model quality.
\citet{longpre2024pretrainer} systematically varied data age, domain coverage, quality, and toxicity across 28 1.5B-parameter models, finding that heterogeneous sources consistently improve downstream performance but that temporal distribution shift degrades it.
\citet{muennighoff2023scaling} extended Chinchilla scaling laws to the data-constrained regime, showing that up to four epochs of data repetition incur negligible loss degradation but that returns diminish sharply beyond this threshold.
On the optimization side, DoReMi~\citep{xie2023doremi} optimizes domain weights through a small proxy model, Data Mixing Laws~\citep{ye2025mixinglaws, data_mixing_laws2024} derive predictive formulas for optimal composition from small-scale experiments, and Aioli~\citep{chen2025aioli} unifies several online mixing strategies under a single framework.
These approaches uniformly evaluate mixing through loss or downstream benchmark scores.
Our work reveals a complementary dimension: the mixing ratio between real and synthetic data reshapes the spectral geometry of internal representations, producing a phase diagram (\S\ref{subsec:phase}) that loss-based metrics alone do not capture.
Our controller further differs in targeting a specific pathology---recursive spectral collapse---through a spectral signal (SLV) rather than optimizing general domain balance.

import sys, json

d = json.load(sys.stdin)
gens = sorted([k for k in d.keys() if k.startswith('gen_')], key=lambda x: int(x.split('_')[1]))

# 提取所有指标
slv = []
ppl = []
eff_rank = []
d4 = []
for g in gens:
    m = d[g]['metrics']
    slv.append(m.get('log_det', None))
    ppl.append(m.get('ppl', None))
    eff_rank.append(m.get('eff_rank', None))
    d4.append(m.get('distinct4', None))

alpha = 0.5

# EMA
ema = [slv[0]]
for t in range(1, len(slv)):
    ema.append(alpha * slv[t] + (1-alpha) * ema[-1])

# Controller signal
S0 = abs(ema[0])
delta = [None]
for t in range(1, len(slv)):
    delta.append((ema[t-1] - ema[t]) / S0)

print('Gen | raw SLV  | EMA SLV  | Δ_t        | PPL    | eff_rank | d4')
for t in range(len(slv)):
    d_str = f'{delta[t]:+.6f}' if delta[t] is not None else '---      '
    p_str = f'{ppl[t]:.3f}' if ppl[t] is not None else 'N/A'
    e_str = f'{eff_rank[t]:.2f}' if eff_rank[t] is not None else 'N/A'
    d4_str = f'{d4[t]:.4f}' if d4[t] is not None else 'N/A'
    print(f'{t:3d} | {slv[t]:8.2f} | {ema[t]:8.2f} | {d_str} | {p_str:>7s} | {e_str:>8s} | {d4_str}')

# Find EMA non-decreasing start
for start in range(2, len(ema)):
    all_nondec = all(ema[i] >= ema[i-1] for i in range(start, len(ema)))
    if all_nondec:
        print(f'\nEMA non-decreasing from Gen {start} onward')
        break

# Summary stats
print(f'\nTotal gens: {len(slv)}')
print(f'Final SLV: {slv[-1]:.2f} (baseline: {slv[0]:.2f}, change: {(slv[-1]-slv[0])/slv[0]*100:+.2f}%)')
if ppl[-1] is not None and ppl[0] is not None:
    print(f'Final PPL: {ppl[-1]:.3f} (baseline: {ppl[0]:.3f}, change: {(ppl[-1]-ppl[0])/ppl[0]*100:+.1f}%)')

pos_deltas = [(t, delta[t]) for t in range(1, len(delta)) if delta[t] is not None and delta[t] > 0]
if pos_deltas:
    max_t, max_d = max(pos_deltas, key=lambda x: x[1])

else:

\paragraph{Model Collapse.}
\citet{shumailov2024collapse} showed that recursive training on model-generated data progressively erodes the tails of learned distributions, a phenomenon they termed \emph{model collapse}.
\citet{dohmatob2024tails} formalized this decay through scaling laws that predict tail erosion as a function of recursive depth, and \citet{dohmatob2024demystified} provided a regression-theoretic analysis of the underlying mechanism.
The self-consuming loop accelerates collapse even under data accumulation~\citep{alemohammad2024mad}, and \citet{dohmatob2025strong} demonstrated that as little as 1\% synthetic contamination suffices to trigger degradation, though \citet{gerstgrasser2024inevitable} showed that preserving all prior real data can delay it.
These studies diagnose collapse through output distributions, benchmark scores, or theoretical scaling laws.
We complement them by tracking collapse through the spectral geometry of internal representations, which requires no text generation or external evaluation.

\paragraph{Spectral Analysis of Representations.}
Random matrix theory (RMT) applied to neural network weights reveals implicit regularization structure in the eigenspectrum~\citep{martin2021implicit}.
Effective rank~\citep{roy2007effectiverank} and its normalized variant RankMe~\citep{rankme2023} have become standard tools for quantifying representational dimensionality.
Recent work has connected spectral properties to training pathologies: \citet{he2025spectral} linked spectral collapse in hidden representations to plasticity loss in continual learning, and \citet{naderi2025mindgap} identified spectral rank collapse in attention matrices as a failure mode of deep transformers.
Most directly relevant, \citet{gu2026sigma} proposed SIGMA, a spectral monitoring framework that tracks singular-value distributions during recursive training on OPT-125M over three generations.
Our work extends SIGMA along several axes.
In \emph{scale}, we track Pythia-410M and pilot Pythia-1B, an order of magnitude larger than OPT-125M.
In \emph{temporal depth}, we follow spectral evolution across 10 recursive generations, revealing a three-phase trajectory (decompression--onset--accelerating collapse) that is not visible at the 3-generation horizon of prior work.
In \emph{methodology}, we move from open-loop observation to closed-loop control: our SLV-based controller actively adjusts the real-data mixing ratio during training (\S\ref{subsec:controller}).
In \emph{metric choice}, we adopt the Spectral Log-Volume (SLV, the log-determinant of the embedding Gram matrix) rather than effective rank or spectral norm, capturing joint changes across the full singular-value spectrum.
Finally, the \emph{signal attenuation paradox}---that successful mixing suppresses the very spectral indicators that would have warned of collapse---is a phenomenon that short-horizon, open-loop monitoring does not encounter.

\paragraph{Early Warning Signals and Critical Transitions.}
The theory of early warning signals (EWS) for critical transitions originates in ecology, where \citet{scheffer2009ews} established that rising autocorrelation and variance precede regime shifts in complex systems.
\citet{scheffer2012anticipating} broadened this framework by identifying architectural features---such as network modularity and feedback structure---that predispose complex systems to tipping points, and argued that combining model-based and observation-based indicators improves anticipation of critical transitions.
\citet{dakos2012methods} developed a methodological toolbox for detecting these signals, and \citet{bury2021deeplearning} showed that deep learning can identify EWS in systems where classical indicators fail.
A central tension in EWS theory is that stabilization interventions suppress the very precursors they rely on~\citep{scheffer2009ews, scheffer2012anticipating}.
We encounter a parallel tension in model collapse, but the failure mode is distinct: ecological stabilization reduces the signal-to-noise ratio while preserving signal direction, whereas real-data mixing reverses the spectral trajectory and eliminates the signal entirely (\S\ref{subsec:controller}).
To our knowledge, this \emph{signal attenuation paradox}---where the intervention that prevents collapse simultaneously destroys the spectral indicator that would have predicted it---has no direct analogue in the ecological EWS literature and constitutes a novel contribution to the broader theory of early warning signals.
\citet{he2025spectral} provides a bridge between these domains by connecting spectral collapse to critical transitions in continual learning.

\paragraph{Data Mixing for LLM Training.}
A growing body of work studies how training data composition shapes language model quality.
\citet{longpre2024pretrainer} systematically varied data age, domain coverage, quality, and toxicity across 28 1.5B-parameter models, finding that heterogeneous sources consistently improve downstream performance but that temporal distribution shift degrades it.
\citet{muennighoff2023scaling} extended Chinchilla scaling laws to the data-constrained regime, showing that up to four epochs of data repetition incur negligible loss degradation but that returns diminish sharply beyond this threshold.
On the optimization side, DoReMi~\citep{xie2023doremi} optimizes domain weights through a small proxy model, Data Mixing Laws~\citep{ye2025mixinglaws, data_mixing_laws2024} derive predictive formulas for optimal composition from small-scale experiments, and Aioli~\citep{chen2025aioli} unifies several online mixing strategies under a single framework.
These approaches uniformly evaluate mixing through loss or downstream benchmark scores.
Our work reveals a complementary dimension: the mixing ratio between real and synthetic data reshapes the spectral geometry of internal representations, producing a phase diagram (\S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram_exp}) that loss-based metrics alone do not capture.
Our controller further differs in targeting a specific pathology---recursive spectral collapse---through a spectral signal (SLV) rather than optimizing general domain balance.

Synthetic data has become integral to language model training.
Instruction tuning, knowledge distillation, and data augmentation all routinely use model-generated text, and as synthetic corpora are recycled into training pipelines, the process often becomes recursive: each generation of models is fine-tuned on outputs from the previous one.
Recent work demonstrates that such recursive synthetic training triggers \textit{model collapse}, a progressive erosion of distributional tails and downstream capability~\citep{shumailov2024collapse, dohmatob2024tails, alemohammad2024mad}.
The problem is especially pressing as web-scraped corpora increasingly contain model-generated content, a trend that introduces implicit recursive loops even without deliberate data reuse.

While model collapse is now well-characterized through theoretical analysis~\citep{dohmatob2024tails} and empirical studies~\citep{shumailov2024collapse, alemohammad2024mad}, its effect on the geometric structure of learned representations remains poorly understood.
Characterizing how the embedding space contracts during recursive training could yield computationally cheap collapse indicators from internal model states alone, without text generation or benchmark evaluation.

Current collapse detection depends on downstream metrics such as perplexity and benchmark accuracy, or on analysis of generated text through lexical diversity measures.
Both approaches require either costly inference or external evaluation infrastructure at every generation.
SIGMA~\citep{gu2026sigma} introduced spectral monitoring through embedding covariance analysis and showed that spectral indicators can track collapse, but validated only on OPT-125M over short generation horizons.
Four gaps remain open.
First, no work has systematically characterized spectral dynamics beyond a few generations at 410M+ parameters.
Second, the temporal relationship between spectral indicators and downstream degradation has not been examined.
Third, no study has connected spectral indicators to closed-loop collapse prevention through the lens of early warning signals (EWS)~\citep{scheffer2009ews}.
Fourth, the relationship between real-data mixing ratios and spectral collapse has not been mapped: it is unknown how much real data suffices to prevent spectral contraction, or whether a sharp phase boundary exists.

We address these gaps by tracking spectral indicators of the embedding Gram matrix across 10 recursive generations of Pythia-410M-deduped~\citep{biderman2023pythia}, with pilot validation on Pythia-1B-deduped.
Our analysis reveals a reproducible three-phase pattern (Figure~\ref{fig:spectral_trajectory}): spectral decompression (Gen~0--2), where effective rank ($r_{\text{eff}}$) and spectral log-volume (SLV) rise while downstream performance already declines; collapse onset (Gen~2--4), where spectral indicators reverse; and accelerating collapse (Gen~4--10), where contraction proceeds at 2.43$\times$ the onset-generation rate.
Among these indicators, SLV is particularly suited for automated monitoring: it requires only a forward pass on held-out data (no text generation), captures distributed volume changes across all spectral directions, and declines monotonically after its peak.
We further design a proof-of-concept proportional controller and discover a signal attenuation paradox: moderate real-data mixing prevents the spectral contraction that would trigger the controller, so reactive spectral feedback becomes ineffective precisely when collapse prevention succeeds.

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{C1:} The first joint spectral-downstream characterization at 410M+ scale: a three-phase collapse pattern (decompression, onset, 2.43$\times$ acceleration) across 10 generations (\S\ref{subsec:phase0}, Table~\ref{tab:phase0}).
\item \textbf{C2:} SLV as a computationally cheap collapse monitor with monotonic post-peak decline and a HellaSwag-spectral asymmetry showing downstream degradation precedes spectral collapse (\S\ref{subsec:phase0}).
\item \textbf{C3:} A signal attenuation paradox: moderate real-data mixing suppresses the spectral signal reactive controllers depend on, a structural limitation formalized via $r_{\text{crit}}$ (\S\ref{subsec:controller}, \S\ref{subsec:phase1}).
\item \textbf{C4:} A spectral collapse phase diagram that maps the boundary between collapse and stability across multiple mixing ratios, and enables empirical localization of $r_{\text{crit}}$ (\S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram}, \S\ref{subsec:phase1}, \S\ref{subsec:phase_diagram_exp}).
\end{itemize}

\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

All experiments use a single random seed; multi-seed replication is needed to establish statistical robustness.
While a second-seed run is in progress, the results reported here reflect a single trajectory per condition, and variance estimates across seeds remain unavailable.

We validate at two model scales only (Pythia-410M and a 1B pilot through Gen~3), leaving open whether the three-phase pattern holds at larger scales or with different architectures.
The 1B pilot covers only three generations, which is sufficient to confirm the decompression peak but insufficient to characterize the full acceleration phase or to estimate $r_{\text{crit}}$ at that scale.

All fine-tuning uses a single data domain (OpenWebText, English web text).
Spectral collapse dynamics may differ substantially for code, multilingual, or domain-specific corpora, where the structure of the data manifold and the degree of distributional shift between real and synthetic text vary.

Ten recursive generations may be shorter than production pipelines, and the spectral trajectory beyond this horizon is unknown.
It is possible that trajectories currently classified as Type~II (transitional) eventually revert to collapse at longer horizons, which would shift the effective $r_{\text{crit}}$ upward.

The adaptive controller uses a simple proportional design with a single gain parameter $k$ and a fixed threshold $\tau$, without integral or derivative terms.
A more sophisticated controller incorporating cumulative drift or rate-of-change signals might partially mitigate the signal attenuation paradox, but exploring such designs is beyond the scope of this work.
